o: For February 2024 (28 days = exactly 4 weeks), report users whose posting count in some 7-consecutive-day window is at least twice their weekly average (total posts / 4). User 3 posted on Feb 6, 14, 25: every 7-day window contains at most 1 post, and 1 < 2 × 0.75, so user 3 is excluded; users with a single post have max window 1 ≥ 2 × 0.25 and are included. The technical challenges are enumerating all 7-day windows (windows may start on any day, anchored at each post date) and producing the average rounded to 4 decimals.
k: avg_weekly_posts = total February posts / 4; max_7day_posts = max over anchors of posts within [anchor, anchor+6].
Anchoring windows at each post date suffices: the maximal window always contains a post at its start.
Filter with HAVING max_7day >= total/2 and round the average to 4 decimals.

a.i: Join February posts to themselves per user where the second post falls within 6 days after the anchor post; grouping by anchor gives each window's count, and MAX over anchors gives the burstiest window.
s: Self-join on user and date range [anchor, anchor + 6 days], count per (user, anchor).
Join with per-user totals, apply HAVING MAX(window) >= total/2, round total/4 to 4 decimals, order by user_id.

c.python:
WITH feb AS (
  SELECT user_id, post_date FROM Posts
  WHERE post_date BETWEEN '2024-02-01' AND '2024-02-28'
), cnt AS (
  SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) c FROM feb GROUP BY user_id
), win AS (
  SELECT f1.user_id, f1.post_date, COUNT(*) m
  FROM feb f1 JOIN feb f2
    ON f1.user_id = f2.user_id
   AND f2.post_date BETWEEN f1.post_date AND DATE_ADD(f1.post_date, INTERVAL 6 DAY)
  GROUP BY f1.user_id, f1.post_date
)
SELECT c.user_id,
       MAX(w.m) AS max_7day_posts,
       ROUND(c.c / 4, 4) AS avg_weekly_posts
FROM cnt c JOIN win w ON c.user_id = w.user_id
GROUP BY c.user_id, c.c
HAVING MAX(w.m) >= c.c / 2
ORDER BY c.user_id;

a.i: Collapse posts to per-day counts first, then build 7-day windows by joining daily rows within 6 days of each anchor day. This shrinks the join input when users post multiple times per day and expresses the logic in terms of a calendar spine.
s: Aggregate February posts to (user_id, post_date, daily_count).
Self-join daily rows within 6 days; sum counts per (user, anchor day).
Combine with totals, filter with HAVING, round, and order.

c.python:
WITH feb AS (
  SELECT user_id, post_date FROM Posts
  WHERE post_date BETWEEN '2024-02-01' AND '2024-02-28'
), daily AS (
  SELECT user_id, post_date, COUNT(*) c
  FROM feb GROUP BY user_id, post_date
), wins AS (
  SELECT d1.user_id, SUM(d2.c) s
  FROM daily d1 JOIN daily d2
    ON d1.user_id = d2.user_id
   AND d2.post_date BETWEEN d1.post_date AND DATE_ADD(d1.post_date, INTERVAL 6 DAY)
  GROUP BY d1.user_id, d1.post_date
), tot AS (
  SELECT user_id, SUM(c) t FROM daily GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT t.user_id,
       COALESCE(MAX(w.s), 0) AS max_7day_posts,
       ROUND(t.t / 4, 4) AS avg_weekly_posts
FROM tot t LEFT JOIN wins w ON t.user_id = w.user_id
GROUP BY t.user_id, t.t
HAVING COALESCE(MAX(w.s), 0) >= t.t / 2
ORDER BY t.user_id;

w: Anchor windows at post dates — anchoring at all 28 calendar days also works but needs a dates spine. Pitfalls: dividing by 28 instead of 4 weeks, comparing against the rounded average instead of the exact ratio, and dropping users via an INNER JOIN where a LEFT JOIN plus COALESCE is intended. Follow-up: generalize to any month (compute weeks = days/7), or define bursts with sliding-window window functions (RANGE BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING).
